n: In this lecture we will talk about synthetic pyrethroids. According to the plan, we will study the representatives cypermethrin, danitol, decis, karate and sumi-alpha, together with the methods of their isolation and analysis. Key words and phrases are given in lecture 15: synthetic pyrethroid derivatives, danitol, cypermethrin, decis. Analytical methods: thin-layer chromatography (TLC), gas-liquid chromatography (GLC), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), GC-MS and UV spectrophotometry.

t: Synthetic pyrethroids: why are they dangerous?
n: Why are synthetic pyrethroids dangerous? Pesticides of this group are highly toxic, with an LD50 of 50-400 mg/kg, and they are widely used, which has led to poisoning of people and animals. One of the causes of fatal outcomes is that there are no approved diagnostic methods or validated analytical procedures for biological fluids and materials. The group includes danitol, cypermethrin, decis, karate, sumi-alpha and others.

On use and production. The pyrethroid pesticides produced at the Navoi Electrochemical Plant have been insufficiently studied from the chemical-toxicological point of view. The group is distinguished by high efficacy, low application rates and a broad action against various species of insects. They are also used against pests of domestic animals and as a disinfectant in medical institutions.

Danitol, that is fenpropathrin, is a complex ester of 2,2,3,3-tetramethylcyclopropanecarboxylic acid and cyano-3-phenoxybenzyl alcohol. It is a white crystalline powder with a melting point of 45-50 °C. It is practically insoluble in water: 0.34 mg/l at 20 °C. It dissolves in methanol, hexane, acetone, chloroform and dimethylformamide, and is resistant to light and heating.

Let us compare the LD50 values of the pyrethroids; all are for oral administration, in mg/kg. Danitol: 49-54 for rats and 58-67 for mice. Cypermethrin: 200-415 for rats and 63 for mice. Decis: 128.5-138.7 mg/kg for rats.

Let us compare the physical properties of the three substances. Danitol: white crystals, melting point 45-50 °C, solubility in water 0.34 mg/l at 20 °C. Cypermethrin: a yellowish oily liquid; practically insoluble in water, 0.03 mg/l. Decis: a white crystalline substance, melting point 98-101 °C, solubility in water 0.002 mg/l at 20 °C.

The toxicological significance of danitol. Abroad it is produced as a 10% emulsifiable concentrate and a 10% suspension concentrate. In Uzbekistan it is produced under the name Uzfen as a 20% emulsifiable concentrate. Danitol is strongly toxic: the oral LD50 is 49-54 mg/kg for rats, 58-67 for mice and 1089 for ducks. It is extremely toxic to aquatic animals: for fish the LC50 is 2.2-9.6 µg/l over 24 hours.

Use of danitol. On cotton fields it is applied against the cotton bollworm, mites and moths at a rate of 1.0-2.0 l/ha. Plants are treated during the growing season; up to four treatments are permitted. It acts on chewing and sucking pests and on caterpillars within several hours and kills them.

Cypermethrin, also known as ripcord, arrivo and cymbush, is cyano-3-phenoxybenzyl 2,2-dimethyl-3-(2,2-dichlorovinyl)cyclopropanecarboxylate. It is a mixture of the cis isomer, 40%, and the trans isomer, 60%: a yellowish oily liquid with a faint odour. The Malaka lecture states that cypermethrin is a liquid with a faint odour, soluble in organic solvents, with an LD50 of 200-415 mg/kg.

Technical cypermethrin, containing 90% of the active substance, is an oily dark-brown liquid and is not volatile. It mixes well with alcohol, ketone, organochlorine and aromatic hydrocarbons; it is practically insoluble in water, 0.03 mg/l. It undergoes hydrolysis under strongly alkaline conditions and is resistant to high temperature. Its density at 25 °C is 1.23 g/cm3; it is stable at pH 5-7. It dissolves well in acetone, xylene, chloroform and cyclohexane.

The toxicity of cypermethrin. It is strongly toxic: the oral LD50 is 200-415 mg/kg for rats and 63 mg/kg for mice. It is not toxic to birds, but acts strongly on bees. For fish the LD50 is 0.0012 mg/l over 96 hours; for the aquatic environment 0.006 mg/l, for soil 0.02 mg/kg. The permissible content in food products is 2.0-0.1 mg/kg.

Use of cypermethrin. It is applied against the cotton bollworm, whitefly, flea beetle, moths, Colorado beetle, thrips and others at a volume of 0.1-1.0 l/ha. It is used to protect greenhouse crops: peppers, cucumbers, tomatoes, carrots and maize. It is also used together with other insecticides and fungicides: on melons, vegetables and in orchards.

Decis, that is deltamethrin, also known as butox and K-othrin, is the cyano-3-phenoxybenzyl ester of dibromovinyl-dimethylcyclopropanecarboxylic acid. It is a white crystalline substance with a melting point of 98-101 °C. It is practically insoluble in water: 0.002 mg/l at 20 °C. It dissolves in acetone, benzene, dimethyl sulfoxide, cyclohexanone and dioxane, and is stable under acidic conditions.

The toxicological significance of decis. It is produced as a 2.5% emulsifiable concentrate, dust, granules and 0.5% ULV solutions. It is strongly toxic to warm-blooded animals: the LD50 is 128.5-138.7 mg/kg for rats and 300 mg/kg for dogs. It has an irritant action on the skin and mucous membranes; in small amounts it accumulates in the body. It is strongly toxic to bees and fish; the permissible concentration in domestic water bodies is 0.006 mg/l, and in soil 0.01 mg/kg.

Let us compare the ecological effects. Danitol is extremely toxic to aquatic animals; for fish the LC50 is 2.2-9.6 µg/l over 24 hours. Cypermethrin is not toxic to birds but acts strongly on bees; for fish the LD50 is 0.0012 mg/l over 96 hours. Decis is strongly toxic to bees and fish; in a water body, 0.006 mg/l.

The inhalation effect and use of decis. By inhalation the LC50 for rats is 60 mg/l; for the wild duck 4640 mg/kg. Against the cotton bollworm, whitefly, flea beetle, moths, Colorado beetle and others it is applied at a volume of 0.1-3.0 l/ha. The preparation Decis FLO is used to protect rape, cabbage, wheat, cotton, sunflower, sugar beet, chickpea and tomato.

Use of karate and sumi-alpha. Karate is used in orchards against fruit-feeding pests, on potatoes against the Colorado beetle, on wheat and barley against grain beetles, and against thrips and flea beetles; the application rate is 0.4-0.8 l/ha. Sumi-alpha is applied against the Colorado beetle, pea aphid, bollworms, moths, flea beetle, mites and thrips; the rate is 0.2-0.5 l/ha. The book lists karate and sumi-alpha as representatives of the pyrethroids and gives no separate description.
The Malaka lecture gives the application rates of pyrethroids in l/ha. Compared with the book: cypermethrin 0.1-1.0, danitol 1.0-2.0, decis 0.1-3.0 l/ha. For karate the rate is 0.4-0.8 l/ha.

Now let us turn to the isolation methods. Isolation from blood: 5 ml of blood is transferred to a conical flask, the pH is adjusted to 8-9 with sodium hydroxide, using universal indicator paper. 2 ml of saturated NaCl and 10 ml of organic solvent are added; the mixture is centrifuged for 5 minutes and the organic layer is collected in a separating funnel. The procedure is repeated twice more; the extracts are combined and filtered, and the solvent is evaporated. The dry residue is examined by TLC, HPLC and UV spectrometry.

Isolation from urine. 25 ml of urine is transferred to a separating funnel, 3 g of NaCl is added, and the pH is adjusted to 8-9 with 0.1 M NaOH. Extraction with organic solvent is carried out three times, with 30, 20 and 20 ml. The extract is passed through a sodium sulphate filter, and the filter is washed with 5 ml of solvent; it is distilled on a rotary evaporator under vacuum until 0.5 ml remains. The residue is transferred to a porcelain dish, the flask is rinsed 2 times with 3 ml of solvent, and the solvent is evaporated in a stream of air.

Isolation from a biological specimen. 10 g of the specimen is minced and mixed with 1-3 ml of water; the pH is adjusted to 9-9.5 with 0.1 M NaOH. 15 ml of organic solvent and 5 ml of saturated NaCl are added; the mixture is left on a shaker for 1 hour. The extraction is repeated twice more; the extract is passed through sodium sulphate and distilled on a rotary evaporator under vacuum. The residue is dried and examined by TLC, UV spectrometry or HPLC.

Let us compare the isolation protocols. For blood: sample 5 ml, pH 8-9, solvent 10 ml, and 3 extractions in total. For urine: 25 ml and 3 g of NaCl, pH 8-9; solvent 30, 20 and 20 ml. For a biological specimen: 10 g, pH 9-9.5; 15 ml of solvent and 5 ml of NaCl, 3 extractions in total.

Extractants and the degree of recovery. Cypermethrin and decis were isolated with chloroform: from urine, 79.50% and 78.56% respectively. Danitol was recovered from urine with ethyl acetate at 78.30%; from blood with hexane-ethyl acetate 1:1 at 67.20%. The degree of extraction from biological material: cypermethrin 50.54%, danitol 50.00%, decis 51.46%.

Let us review the degree of extraction for each pyrethroid. Cypermethrin: urine 79.50%, blood 75.66%, biological material 50.54%, with chloroform. Danitol: urine 78.30%, blood 67.20%, here with hexane-ethyl acetate 1:1, and biological material 50.00%, with ethyl acetate. Decis: urine 78.56%, blood 77.60%, biological material 51.46%, with chloroform.

Plates and sorbents for TLC. For danitol, a Silufol plate and Silpearl sorbent are used. For cypermethrin, a laboratory-prepared silica gel plate, silica gel LS 5/40 µm. For sumi-alpha, decis and karate, Silufol and Sorbfil are used; the Sorbfil types are STKh-1VE, 8-12 µm, and STKh-1A, 5-17 µm.

Visualising reagents in TLC. For danitol, Marquis reagent is used. For cypermethrin, zinc chloride-iodine, that is ClZnI, and Dragendorff reagent modified by Munier. For sumi-alpha, decis and karate, a 1% aqueous solution of sodium eosinate and modified bromophenol blue are used.

Rf values in TLC. Cypermethrin: 0.44 in hexane-acetone 5:1; 0.58 in chloroform-methanol 7:1; 0.61 in hexane-ethyl acetate 3:1. Danitol: 0.55 in hexane-acetone 2:1 and 0.47 in hexane-ethyl acetate 3:1. Sumi-alpha: 0.68 in hexane-chloroform 2:1; karate: 0.57 in chloroform-hexane 2:1; decis 0.6 at 3:2.

Detection limits. Cypermethrin: 2 µg with Dragendorff reagent modified by Munier; 1.5 µg with zinc chloride-iodine reagent. Danitol: 2 µg with Marquis reagent. Sumi-alpha, decis and karate: 2 µg with a 1% solution of sodium eosinate; 2.5 µg with a 0.5% solution of bromophenol blue.

GLC conditions. Column: Chromaton N-AW-DMCS sorbent impregnated with 5% SE-30, glass, 130 x 0.2 cm; carrier gas nitrogen, 30 ml/min. Hydrogen and air flows are 30 ml/min and 350 ml/min respectively. Oven programme: from 180 to 220 °C at 10 °C/min, then to 245 °C at 3 °C/min. Detector temperature 260 °C, injector temperature 250 °C.

The Malaka lecture gives a table of retention times of pesticides in GLC, in minutes. Sevin 6.9, danitol 10.2, sumi-alpha 14.1, cypermethrin 15.3. Hexachlorane was not detected under these conditions.

Instrument and column for HPLC. An Agilent 1100 series chromatograph from Agilent Technologies is used, controlled by Chemstation A.09.03 software. It has a four-channel gradient pump, a degasser and a UV/VIS spectrophotometric detector operating at 190-600 nm. Column: 150 x 3 mm, particle size 3.5 µm, Zorbax Eclipse XDB C-18 sorbent.

The mobile phase in HPLC. The optimal composition: phosphate buffer at pH 3.0, A, and acetonitrile, B, with a linear gradient. Gradient: at 0 minutes A 80%, B 20%; at 7-20 minutes A 25%, B 75%; at 24 minutes again A 80%, B 20%. Flow rate 0.5 ml/min; analysis at 278-280 nm, duration 24 minutes.

Retention times in HPLC. The retention time of danitol is 17.4 minutes. Cypermethrin and its isomers elute at 18.7 and 19.7 minutes; decis at 20.1 minutes. Sumi-alpha at 20.9, and karate at 21.9 minutes.

UV spectrophotometry. The method is carried out at a layer thickness of 10 mm in the 200-400 nm range; the reference solution is the corresponding organic solvents. Pyrethroids absorb light with a single maximum in the 260-280 nm region. The specific and molar absorbance values of cypermethrin, danitol and decis lie in the ranges 82.0-91.0 and 3195.0-4405.1 respectively. The method obeys the Bouguer-Lambert-Beer law at concentrations of 10-100 µg/ml.

Procedures have been developed for the analysis of synthetic pyrethroids by TLC, GLC, HPLC, GC-MS and UV spectrophotometry. The Malaka lecture shows that in HPLC danitol elutes at 17.2 minutes and the cypermethrin isomers at 18.5 and 19.1 minutes. The dry residue isolated from blood, urine and specimens is examined by TLC, HPLC and UV spectrometry.

The general scheme of pyrethroid analysis. Isolation is carried out by a separate protocol for blood, urine and a biological specimen; pH 8-9 and 9-9.5, with NaCl. Confirmation is carried out first by TLC, that is by reagent and Rf, then by GLC, HPLC, GC-MS and the UV spectrum. Factors affecting the result: a degree of extraction of 50-79% and a detection limit of 1.5-2.5 µg.

Let us once more recall the order in which the substances elute in HPLC. First danitol elutes at 17.4 minutes; then the cypermethrin isomers at 18.7 and 19.7 minutes. Then decis at 20.1, sumi-alpha at 20.9 and karate at 21.9 minutes. Analysis is carried out at 278-280 nm; duration 24 minutes.

Let us conclude. Synthetic pyrethroids, that is danitol, cypermethrin, decis, karate and sumi-alpha, are highly toxic, with an LD50 of 50-400 mg/kg; approved methods are lacking. Isolation is carried out from blood, urine and specimens with an organic solvent at pH 8-9.5; the degree of extraction is 50-79%. In the analysis TLC is used: with Marquis, ClZnI and Dragendorff reagents, eosinate and bromophenol blue. GLC, HPLC, at 278-280 nm, and the UV spectrum, at 260-280 nm, are also used. They are strongly toxic to bees and fish and hazardous to the environment.
